claim: Land plants are characterized by the alternation of haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) phases within their lifecycle, both of which are multicellular.
source: Land plants are characterized by the alternation of haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) phases within their lifecycle, both of which are multicellular (Niklas and Kutschera, 2010; Bowman et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Niklas and Kutschera, 2010; Bowman et al., 2016) and represents established scientific knowledge about land plant lifecycles.

claim: In the earliest diverging bryophyte lineages (liverworts, mosses and hornworts) the free-living indeterminate gametophyte predominates the lifecycle.
source: In the earliest diverging bryophyte lineages (liverworts, mosses and hornworts) the free-living indeterminate gametophyte predominates the lifecycle, producing gametes that fuse to form the sporophyte.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bryophyte biology, representing a well-known characteristic of these plant lineages.

claim: The bryophyte sporophyte embryo develops on the surface of the gametophyte, ultimately forming a simple determinate spore-producing axis.
source: The sporophyte embryo develops on the surface of the gametophyte, ultimately forming a simple determinate spore-producing axis (Kato and Akiyama, 2005; Ligrone et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kato and Akiyama, 2005; Ligrone et al., 2012).

claim: Angiosperm sporophytes range from small herbaceous to large arborescent forms, all developing from an indeterminate vegetative shoot apex that ultimately transitions to flowering.
source: By contrast, angiosperm (flowering plant) sporophytes range from small herbaceous to large arborescent forms, all developing from an indeterminate vegetative shoot apex that ultimately transitions to flowering, and gametophytes are few-celled determinate structures produced within flowers (Schmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Schmidt et al., 2015) and represents established knowledge about angiosperm development.

claim: Angiosperm gametophytes are few-celled determinate structures produced within flowers.
source: By contrast, angiosperm (flowering plant) sporophytes range from small herbaceous to large arborescent forms, all developing from an indeterminate vegetative shoot apex that ultimately transitions to flowering, and gametophytes are few-celled determinate structures produced within flowers (Schmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Schmidt et al., 2015) and represents established knowledge about angiosperm gametophyte structure.

claim: A prolonged and plastic phase of vegetative development arose in the sporophyte of all vascular plants (lycophytes, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms).
source: A series of developmental innovations during the course of land plant evolution thus simplified gametophyte form whilst increasing sporophyte complexity, with a prolonged and plastic phase of vegetative development arising in the sporophyte of all vascular plants (lycophytes, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis of developmental patterns across vascular plant lineages, representing established knowledge in plant evolution.

claim: A single bHLH transcription factor in the moss Physcomitrella patens regulates stomatal differentiation.
source: For example, a single bHLH transcription factor in the moss Physcomitrella patens regulates stomatal differentiation, whereas gene duplications have resulted in three homologs with sub-divided stomatal patterning roles in the angiosperm Arabidopsis thaliana (hereafter 'Arabidopsis') (MacAlister and Bergmann, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (MacAlister and Bergmann, 2011).

claim: Gene duplications have resulted in three bHLH homologs with sub-divided stomatal patterning roles in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: For example, a single bHLH transcription factor in the moss Physcomitrella patens regulates stomatal differentiation, whereas gene duplications have resulted in three homologs with sub-divided stomatal patterning roles in the angiosperm Arabidopsis thaliana (hereafter 'Arabidopsis') (MacAlister and Bergmann, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (MacAlister and Bergmann, 2011).

claim: Class III HD-ZIP transcription factors play a conserved role in the regulation of leaf polarity in P. patens and Arabidopsis.
source: class III HD-ZIP transcription factors play a conserved role in the regulation of leaf polarity in P. patens and Arabidopsis but gene family members have acquired regulatory activity in meristems of angiosperms (Yip et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yip et al., 2016).

claim: Class III HD-ZIP gene family members have acquired regulatory activity in meristems of angiosperms.
source: class III HD-ZIP transcription factors play a conserved role in the regulation of leaf polarity in P. patens and Arabidopsis but gene family members have acquired regulatory activity in meristems of angiosperms (Yip et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yip et al., 2016).

claim: The gene regulatory network that produces rhizoids on the gametophytes of P. patens and M. polymorpha has been co-opted to regulate root hair formation in Arabidopsis sporophytes.
source: and the gene regulatory network that produces rhizoids on the gametophytes of both the moss P. patens and the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha has been co-opted to regulate root hair formation in Arabidopsis sporophytes (Menand et al., 2007; Pires et al., 2013; Proust et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Menand et al., 2007; Pires et al., 2013; Proust et al., 2016).

claim: The LEAFY gene family is present as a single gene copy in most land plant genomes.
source: The LFY gene family is present as a single gene copy in most land plant genomes (Sayou et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sayou et al., 2014).

claim: In P. patens, LFY regulates cell divisions during sporophyte development (including the first division of the zygote).
source: In P. patens, LFY regulates cell divisions during sporophyte development (including the first division of the zygote) (Tanahashi et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tanahashi et al., 2005).

claim: In angiosperms the major role of LFY is to promote the transition from inflorescence to floral meristem identity.
source: whereas in angiosperms the major role is to promote the transition from inflorescence to floral meristem identity (Carpenter and Coen, 1990; Schultz, 1991; Weigel et al., 1992; Blázquez et al., 1997; Souer et al., 1998; Molinero-Rosales et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Carpenter and Coen, 1990; Schultz, 1991; Weigel et al., 1992; Blázquez et al., 1997; Souer et al., 1998; Molinero-Rosales et al., 1999).

claim: LFY proteins from liverworts and all vascular plant lineages tested to date (ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms) bind a conserved target DNA motif.
source: Given that LFY proteins from liverworts and all vascular plant lineages tested to date (ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms) bind a conserved target DNA motif, whereas hornwort and moss homologs bind to different lineage-specific motifs (Sayou et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sayou et al., 2014).

claim: Hornwort and moss LFY homologs bind to different lineage-specific DNA motifs.
source: Given that LFY proteins from liverworts and all vascular plant lineages tested to date (ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms) bind a conserved target DNA motif, whereas hornwort and moss homologs bind to different lineage-specific motifs (Sayou et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sayou et al., 2014).

claim: PpLFY cannot complement loss-of-function lfy mutants in Arabidopsis.
source: This suggestion is supported by the observation that PpLFY cannot complement loss-of-function lfy mutants in Arabidopsis (Maizel et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Maizel et al., 2005).

claim: The lfy mutant is not complemented by lycophyte LFY proteins.
source: Similar complementation studies indicate progressive functional changes as vascular plant lineages diverged in that the lfy mutant is not complemented by lycophyte LFY proteins (Yang et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yang et al., 2017).

claim: The lfy mutant is partially and progressively complemented by fern and gymnosperm LFY homologs.
source: but is partially and progressively complemented by fern and gymnosperm homologs (Maizel et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Maizel et al., 2005).

claim: Ceratopteris richardii contains two LFY genes.
source: In this regard, the presence of two LFY genes in Ceratopteris (Himi et al., 2001) is atypical.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Himi et al., 2001).

claim: The two gene copies identified in Equisetum arvense, Azolla caroliniana and Ceratopteris each resulted from recent independent duplication events.
source: Within the ferns (64 in total), phylogenetic relationships between LFY sequences indicated that the two gene copies identified in Equisetum arvense, Azolla caroliniana and Ceratopteris each resulted from recent independent duplication events (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 1, which shows the evolutionary relationships between LFY sequences in ferns.

claim: The Ceratopteris genome contains no more than two copies of LFY.
source: Gel blot analysis confirmed the presence of no more than two LFY genes in the Ceratopteris genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gel blot analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 are equally orthologous to the single copy LFY representatives in other fern species.
source: Given that the topology of the tree excludes the possibility of a gene duplication prior to diversification of the ferns, CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 are equally orthologous to the single copy LFY representatives in other fern species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic tree topology, which shows that the duplication occurred after fern diversification.

claim: CrLFY2 transcript levels were similar across sporophyte samples.
source: Whereas CrLFY2 transcript levels were similar across sporophyte samples, CrLFY1 transcript levels were much higher in samples that contained the shoot apex (Figure 3F,G) than in those that contained just fronds (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: CrLFY1 transcript levels were much higher in samples that contained the shoot apex than in those that contained just fronds.
source: Whereas CrLFY2 transcript levels were similar across sporophyte samples, CrLFY1 transcript levels were much higher in samples that contained the shoot apex (Figure 3F,G) than in those that contained just fronds (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 genes may play divergent roles during sporophyte development, with CrLFY1 acting primarily in the shoot apex and CrLFY2 acting more generally.
source: These data suggest that CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 genes may play divergent roles during sporophyte development, with CrLFY1 acting primarily in the shoot apex and CrLFY2 acting more generally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns observed in qRT-PCR data (Figure 3L).

claim: No GUS activity was detected in unfertilized archegonia of CrLFY1pro::GUS gametophytes.
source: Notably, no GUS activity was detected in unfertilized archegonia of CrLFY1pro::GUS gametophytes (Figure 4A,F,K)
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 4A, F, K.

claim: By two days after fertilization (DAF) GUS activity was detected in most cells of the early sporophyte embryo.
source: but by two days after fertilization (DAF) GUS activity was detected in most cells of the early sporophyte embryo (Figure 4B,G,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 4B, G, L.

claim: At 4 DAF, GUS activity was detected in all visible embryo cells, including the embryonic frond, but not in the surrounding gametophytic tissue (the calyptra).
source: At 4 DAF, activity was similarly detected in all visible embryo cells, including the embryonic frond, but not in the surrounding gametophytic tissue (the calyptra) (Figure 4C,H,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 4C, H, M.

claim: By the end of embryogenesis (6 DAF) GUS activity was predominantly localized in the newly-initiated shoot apex.
source: This embryo-wide pattern of GUS activity became restricted in the final stages of development such that by the end of embryogenesis (6 DAF) GUS activity was predominantly localized in the newly-initiated shoot apex (Figure 4D,E,I,J,N,O).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 4D, E, I, J, N, O.

claim: CrLFY1 expression is induced following formation of the zygote, sustained in cells of the embryo that are actively dividing, and then restricted to the shoot apex at embryo maturity.
source: Collectively, the GUS activity profiles indicate that CrLFY1 expression is induced following formation of the zygote, sustained in cells of the embryo that are actively dividing, and then restricted to the shoot apex at embryo maturity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GUS activity patterns observed across developmental stages (Figure 4).

claim: CrLFY1 has retained the LFY role first identified in P. patens, namely to promote the development of a multicellular sporophyte, in part by facilitating the first cell division of the zygote.
source: This profile is consistent with the suggestion that CrLFY1 has retained the LFY role first identified in P. patens (Tanahashi et al., 2005), namely to promote the development of a multicellular sporophyte, in part by facilitating the first cell division of the zygote.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern data and comparison with known P. patens LFY function, supported by citation (Tanahashi et al., 2005).

claim: In young sporophytes (20 DAF), GUS activity was primarily localized in shoot apical tissues and newly-emerging frond primordia.
source: In young sporophytes (20 DAF), GUS activity was primarily localized in shoot apical tissues and newly-emerging frond primordia (Figure 5A,F,K), with very little activity detected in the expanded simple fronds produced at this age (Figure 5B,G,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 5A, F, K, B, G, L.

claim: In older vegetative sporophytes (60 DAF), GUS activity was localized in the shoot apex and young frond primordia in two out of the three fully characterized lines.
source: In older vegetative sporophytes (60 DAF), which develop complex dissected fronds (Figure 5C,H,M), GUS activity was similarly localized in the shoot apex and young frond primordia in two out of the three fully characterized lines (Figure 5D,I,N) and in a total of 8 out of 11 lines screened (from seven independent rounds of plant transformation).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 5D, I, N.

claim: GUS activity was detected in developing fronds in regions where the lamina was dividing to generate pinnae and pinnules.
source: GUS activity was also detected in developing fronds in regions where the lamina was dividing to generate pinnae and pinnules (Figure 5E,J,O).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 5E, J, O.

claim: Patterns of CrLFY1pro::GUS expression were the same in the apex and complex fronds of shoots before (60 DAF) and after (~115 DAF) the reproductive transition.
source: Notably, patterns of CrLFY1pro::GUS expression were the same in the apex and complex fronds of shoots before (60 DAF) (Figure 5C–E,H–J,M–O) and after (~115 DAF) the reproductive transition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GUS activity was detected in shoot apices that initiate de novo at the lamina margin between pinnae.
source: Consistent with a general role for CrLFY1 in promoting cell proliferation in the shoot, GUS activity was also detected in shoot apices that initiate de novo at the lamina margin between pinnae (Figure 5Z–AD).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS staining data shown in Figure 5Z–AD.

claim: LFY function was recruited to regulate cell division processes in the shoot when sporophytes evolved from determinate to indeterminate structures.
source: Together these data support the hypothesis that LFY function was recruited to regulate cell division processes in the shoot when sporophytes evolved from determinate to indeterminate structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern data showing LFY activity in dividing tissues throughout shoot development.

claim: All four RNAi constructs led to suppressed transcript levels of both CrLFY genes.
source: Despite the predicted sequence specificity of CrLFY1-i3 and CrLFY2-i4 (Supplementary file 5), qRT-PCR analysis found that all four RNAi constructs led to suppressed transcript levels of both CrLFY genes (Figure 6R,S).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6R, S.

claim: The severity of the shoot phenotype was correlated with the level of endogenous CrLFY transcripts detected across all lines.
source: The severity of the shoot phenotype was correlated with the level of endogenous CrLFY transcripts detected across all lines (Figure 6R,S)
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6R, S and phenotypic observations.

claim: Relative levels of both CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 were significantly reduced compared to controls in all early-terminating sporophytes (p<0.01 or less).
source: with relative levels of both CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 significantly reduced compared to controls in all early-terminating sporophytes (E8, G13, C3, D2, D4a, D13, F9) (p<0.01 or less).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and statistical analysis (Figure 6R, S).

claim: In phenotypically normal transgenic siblings CrLFY2 transcript levels were not significantly lower than controls.
source: In phenotypically normal transgenic siblings CrLFY2 transcript levels were not significantly lower than controls (indeed in line D2, levels were higher p<0.01) whereas CrLFY1 levels were significantly reduced (p<0.0001), as in arrested siblings.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data and statistical analysis (Figure 6R, S).

claim: CrLFY2 can compensate for some loss of CrLFY1.
source: Together, these data indicate that CrLFY2 can compensate for some loss of CrLFY1, but at least 22% of CrLFY1 activity is required for normal development (line D4a pn, Figure 6J,S).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phenotypically normal plants can be obtained with reduced CrLFY1 levels if CrLFY2 levels are normal.

claim: At least 22% of CrLFY1 activity is required for normal development.
source: Together, these data indicate that CrLFY2 can compensate for some loss of CrLFY1, but at least 22% of CrLFY1 activity is required for normal development (line D4a pn, Figure 6J,S).
evidence: This is an inference based on qRT-PCR data showing the minimum CrLFY1 expression level in phenotypically normal plants.

claim: CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 act partially redundantly to maintain indeterminacy of the shoot apex in Ceratopteris.
source: It can thus be concluded that CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 act partially redundantly to maintain indeterminacy of the shoot apex in Ceratopteris, a role not found in the early divergent bryophyte P. patens, nor known to be retained in the majority of later diverging flowering plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi phenotypes and expression data, showing that both genes contribute to shoot apex maintenance.

claim: In six of the RNAi lines that exhibited sporophyte developmental defects, 50–99% of gametophytes arrested development prior to the sporophyte phase of the lifecycle.
source: In six of the RNAi lines that exhibited sporophyte developmental defects, it was notable that 50–99% of gametophytes arrested development prior to the sporophyte phase of the lifecycle (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations summarized in Table 1.

claim: LFY plays a role in Ceratopteris gametophyte development.
source: This observation suggested that LFY plays a role in Ceratopteris gametophyte development, a function not previously demonstrated in either bryophytes or angiosperms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gametophyte arrest phenotypes observed in RNAi lines.

claim: The gametophytes from six RNAi lines exhibited developmental arrest, which in five lines clearly related to a failure of AC activity.
source: In contrast, the gametophytes from six RNAi lines (carrying either ZmUbipro::CrLFY1-i3, ZmUbipro::CrLFY1/2-i1 or ZmUbipro::CrLFY1/2-i2) exhibited developmental arrest (Figure 7D–J), which in five lines clearly related to a failure of AC activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 7D–J.

claim: CrLFY transcripts were detected in the AC and immediate daughter cells of wild-type gametophytes by in situ hybridization.
source: A role for CrLFY in maintenance of gametophyte AC activity was supported by the detection of CrLFY transcripts in the AC and immediate daughter cells of wild-type gametophytes by in situ hybridization (Figure 7K–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7K–N.

claim: CrLFY transcripts were not detected in arrested ZmUbipro::CrLFY1/2-i1 lines.
source: By contrast CrLFY transcripts were not detected in arrested ZmUbipro::CrLFY1/2-i1 lines (Figure 7O–R) in which the presence of the transgene was confirmed by genotyping of individual arrested gametophytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7O–R and genotyping data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: At least one CrLFY homolog plays a role in AC maintenance during gametophyte development.
source: However, these data support a role for at least one CrLFY homolog in AC maintenance during gametophyte development, and thus invoke a role for LFY in the regulation of apical activity in both the sporophyte and gametophyte phases of vascular plant development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gametophyte phenotypes and in situ hybridization data.

claim: CrLFY has a role in maintaining cell divisions in the apical stem cells of both haploid and diploid phases of the lifecycle.
source: Here, we report a transgenic analysis in the fern Ceratopteris richardii that reveals a role for LEAFY in maintaining cell divisions in the apical stem cells of both haploid and diploid phases of the lifecycle.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined data from reporter lines, RNAi phenotypes, and in situ hybridization across both gametophyte and sporophyte phases.

claim: An ancestral LEAFY module that promotes cell proliferation was progressively co-opted, adapted and specialized as novel shoot developmental contexts emerged.
source: These results support an evolutionary trajectory in which an ancestral LEAFY module that promotes cell proliferation was progressively co-opted, adapted and specialized as novel shoot developmental contexts emerged.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the functional data from Ceratopteris combined with comparative analysis across land plant lineages.

claim: qRT-PCR and transgenic reporter lines demonstrated that CrLFY1 is preferentially expressed in the shoot apex.
source: During sporophyte development, qRT-PCR and transgenic reporter lines demonstrated that CrLFY1 is preferentially expressed in the shoot apex (whether formed during embryogenesis or de novo on fronds, and both before and after the reproductive transition)
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 3) and GUS reporter data (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: CrLFY1 is expressed in emerging lateral organ (frond) primordia.
source: in emerging lateral organ (frond) primordia; and in pinnae and pinnules as they form on dissected fronds (Figures 3–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 3) and GUS reporter data (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: Active cell division is the main feature in all contexts where CrLFY1 is expressed.
source: Notably, active cell division is the main feature in all of these contexts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between CrLFY1 expression patterns and known sites of active cell division.

claim: CrLFY2 transcript levels were more uniform throughout sporophyte shoot development, in both dividing tissues and expanded fronds.
source: CrLFY2 transcript levels were more uniform throughout sporophyte shoot development, in both dividing tissues and expanded fronds (Figure 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CrLFY2 expression has been reported in roots.
source: and expression has previously been reported in roots (Himi et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Himi et al., 2001).

claim: Simultaneous suppression of CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 activity by RNAi resulted in developmental arrest of both gametophyte and sporophyte shoot apices.
source: Simultaneous suppression of CrLFY1 and CrLFY2 activity by RNAi resulted in developmental arrest of both gametophyte and sporophyte shoot apices, with any fronds produced before termination of the sporophyte apex exhibiting abnormal morphologies (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Wild-type levels of CrLFY2 are able to fully compensate for up to a 70% reduction in CrLFY1 levels.
source: with wild-type levels of CrLFY2 able to fully compensate for up to a 70% reduction in CrLFY1 levels (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and phenotypic data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The duplicate CrLFY genes act at least partially redundantly during shoot development in Ceratopteris.
source: The duplicate CrLFY genes therefore act at least partially redundantly during shoot development in Ceratopteris.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CrLFY2 can compensate for reduced CrLFY1 levels.

claim: A function for LFY in gametophyte development has not previously been reported in any land plant species.
source: A function for LFY in gametophyte development has not previously been reported in any land plant species.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, representing what has been published in the literature.

claim: In P. patens, PpLFY1 and PpLFY2 are expressed in both the main and lateral apices of gametophytic leafy shoots.
source: In the moss P. patens, PpLFY1 and PpLFY2 are expressed in both the main and lateral apices of gametophytic leafy shoots but double loss-offunction mutants develop normally, indicating that LFY is not necessary for maintenance of apical cell activity in the gametophyte (Tanahashi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tanahashi et al., 2005).

claim: Double loss-of-function mutants of PpLFY1 and PpLFY2 develop normally, indicating that LFY is not necessary for maintenance of apical cell activity in the P. patens gametophyte.
source: In the moss P. patens, PpLFY1 and PpLFY2 are expressed in both the main and lateral apices of gametophytic leafy shoots but double loss-offunction mutants develop normally, indicating that LFY is not necessary for maintenance of apical cell activity in the gametophyte (Tanahashi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Tanahashi et al., 2005).

claim: Loss of CrLFY expression from the gametophyte shoot apex results in loss of apical cell activity during thallus formation in Ceratopteris.
source: By contrast, loss of CrLFY expression from the gametophyte shoot apex results in loss of apical cell activity during thallus formation in Ceratopteris (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The different DNA binding site preferences of PpLFY and CrLFY may be sufficient to explain the functional distinction in moss and fern gametophytes.
source: The different DNA binding site preferences (and hence downstream target sequences) of PpLFY and CrLFY (Sayou et al., 2014) may be sufficient to explain the functional distinction in moss and fern gametophytes
evidence: This is speculation based on known differences in DNA binding preferences, supported by citation (Sayou et al., 2014).

claim: In the last common ancestor of ferns and angiosperms, LFY functioned to promote cell proliferation in the thalloid gametophyte.
source: Overall the data are consistent with the hypothesis that in the last common ancestor of ferns and angiosperms, LFY functioned to promote cell proliferation in the thalloid gametophyte, a role that has been lost in angiosperms where gametophytes have no apical cell and are instead just few-celled determinate structures.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the functional data from Ceratopteris and comparative analysis with angiosperms.

claim: The ancestral LFY function to promote early cell divisions in the embryo was retained in vascular plants after they diverged from the bryophytes.
source: First, the ancestral LFY function to promote early cell divisions in the embryo was retained in vascular plants after they diverged from the bryophytes, leading to conserved roles in P. patens (Tanahashi et al., 2005) and Ceratopteris (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on functional data from both P. patens (cited) and Ceratopteris (Figure 4).

claim: Within the vascular plants, the proliferative role of LFY expanded to maintain post-embryonic apical cell activity, and hence to enable indeterminate shoot growth.
source: Second, within the vascular plants (preceding divergence of the ferns) this proliferative role expanded to maintain post-embryonic apical cell activity, and hence to enable indeterminate shoot growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data from Ceratopteris showing LFY activity in post-embryonic shoot apices.

claim: CrLFY activity is detected at the tips of shoots, fronds and pinnae, all of which develop from one or more apical cells.
source: This is evidenced by CrLFY activity at the tips of shoots, fronds and pinnae (Figures 4–6), all of which develop from one or more apical cells (Hill, 2001; Hou and Hill, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by GUS reporter data (Figures 4–6) and citations to published literature on apical cell development (Hill, 2001; Hou and Hill, 2004).

claim: There are angiosperm examples of LFY function in the vegetative SAM.
source: but there are angiosperm examples of LFY function in the vegetative SAM (Ahearn et al., 2001; Zhao et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ahearn et al., 2001; Zhao et al., 2018).

claim: There are angiosperm examples of LFY function in axillary meristems.
source: axillary meristems (Kanrar et al., 2008; Rao et al., 2008; Chahtane et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kanrar et al., 2008; Rao et al., 2008; Chahtane et al., 2013).

claim: There are angiosperm examples of LFY function in actively dividing regions of compound leaves.
source: and in actively dividing regions of compound leaves (Hofer et al., 1997; Molinero-Rosales et al., 1999; Champagne et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2008; Monniaux et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hofer et al., 1997; Molinero-Rosales et al., 1999; Champagne et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2008; Monniaux et al., 2017).

claim: A proliferative role for LFY in vegetative tissues has been retained in at least some angiosperm species.
source: indicating that a proliferative role in vegetative tissues has been retained in at least some angiosperm species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited examples of LFY function in vegetative tissues of angiosperms.

claim: The angiosperm floral meristem represents a modified vegetative meristem.
source: Consistent with the suggestion that the angiosperm floral meristem represents a modified vegetative meristem (Theiben et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Theiben et al., 2016).
